title: Booting a machine with no disk
description: How a computer with nothing but a hardware address learns who it is on the network, from ARP and RARP through BOOTP and DHCP to DHCPv6.
questions: how does a diskless computer get an ip address
how does a computer get an ip address when it boots
what is the difference between rarp bootp and dhcp
how does a computer load its operating system over the network

steps.title: Find your neighbours
steps.subtitle: ARP
steps.description: Before any host can send an IP packet on Ethernet it has to turn the destination IP address into a hardware address. ARP does that by asking the whole segment, and RARP reuses its packet format.

steps.title: Ask for your own address
steps.subtitle: RARP
steps.description: A machine that knows only its hardware address broadcasts a request and a server that holds a hardware-to-IP table answers. It works on one network segment and returns only an address.

steps.title: Make it routable
steps.subtitle: BOOTP
steps.description: BOOTP carries the same idea over UDP and IP so requests can be relayed across routers, and the reply can also name a server and a boot file. RFC 1542 clarified how BOOTP behaves across relays.

steps.title: Fetch the boot image
steps.subtitle: TFTP
steps.description: With an address and a boot file name in hand, a diskless machine typically downloads its operating system image over TFTP, a deliberately tiny file-transfer protocol that fits in a boot ROM.

steps.title: Leases and options
steps.subtitle: DHCP
steps.description: DHCP grew out of BOOTP. It hands out addresses for a limited time, so they can be reclaimed, and carries a long list of options such as gateway, DNS servers and domain name.

steps.title: The IPv6 successor
steps.subtitle: DHCPv6
steps.description: IPv6 hosts can configure themselves, but DHCPv6 still hands out addresses and options where administrators want control. DHCPv6 was revised as RFC 8415 and then again as RFC 9915.
